title: The Broken Earthen Water Pot (PT)
summary: A servant weeps uncontrollably after breaking an antique water pot. Birbal uses the broken pieces to teach the court the wisdom of moving forward. [PT]
full_text:
A young palace servant named Mohan was carrying an antique earthenware water pot, painted with intricate Persian motifs, through the council hallway when his foot caught on a carpet. The pot crashed to the marble floor, shattering into dozens of fragments, spilling water across the stones.

Terrified of punishment, the young servant collapsed beside the shards, weeping hysterically, tearing his hair, and crying: 'Oh, my life is ruined! If only I had looked at the carpet! If only I had walked slower! If only I had taken the other corridor!'

For an hour, the servant remained paralyzed on the floor in useless sorrow.

Birbal walked down the hallway, knelt beside the weeping youth, picked up a handful of broken clay shards, and asked:

'Mohan, look at these shards in my hand. Can all your bitter tears reassemble this pot?'

The boy sniffled: 'No, my lord.'

'Can all your weeping dry the spilled water back into the pitcher?'

'No, my lord.'

'Can beating your chest undo the step you took an hour ago?'

'No, wise minister.'

Birbal helped the youth to his feet, handed him a broom and a mop, and said with gentle firmness:

'Then stand up, my boy, wipe your tears, and pick up the broom!

'What is broken is broken. What has passed has passed into eternity. Crying over spilled water does not clean the floor; it merely wastes the hours of today on the regrets of yesterday!

'Sweep away the shards, dry the stones, and walk forward with greater care. The wise man does not mourn what is shattered; he applies his energy to building what lies ahead.'

The young servant smiled through his tears, cleaned the floor diligently, and returned to his duties with a peaceful heart. Akbar, who had observed the scene, remarked that Birbal's practical wisdom was the greatest medicine for human regret.
